content.text: Ancient Dynasties of Andhra: Satavahanas to Eastern Chalukyas, Art, Religion, and the Genesis of Telugu

The ancient history of Andhra Pradesh (c. 3rd century BCE – 11th century CE) represents the foundation of Telugu linguistic and cultural identity. Anchored by the Satavahana empire along the fertile Krishna-Godavari doab, Andhra evolved into an international hub for Buddhist scholasticism and maritime commerce, before transitioning through the Ikshvakus, Vishnukundins, Renati Cholas, and Eastern Chalukyas into classical Telugu literature and temple architecture.
1. The Satavahanas (Andhrabhrityas): Empire, Society, and Economy

Mentioned in the Aitareya Brahmana and Puranas, the Satavahana dynasty was established by Simuka after Mauryan decline, establishing capitals at Kotilingala (Telangana), Pratishthana (Paithan, Maharashtra), and Dhanyakataka (Amaravati / Dharanikota, AP):

content.caption: Key Satavahana Monarchs, Epigraphs, and Milestones
rows: Performed two Ashvamedhas, one Rajasuya; first recorded ruler to make tax-free land grants (Brahmadeya) to Buddhist monks and Brahmins; assumed title 'Dakshinapathapati'.

Compiled 700 erotic and pastoral stanzas in Maharashtri Prakrit, containing numerous Desi Telugu words (e.g., Atta, Pilla, Vangi, Poddu); celebrated by poet Gunadhya (who composed 'Brihatkatha' in Paisachi Prakrit) and Sarvavarma (Katantra Sanskrit Grammar).
Nasik Prashasti of Queen Mother Gautami Balasri

Greatest Satavahana emperor (reigned c. 106–130 CE); crushed the Western Kshatrapa king Nahapana (restruck Jogalthambi coin hoard); titles: 'Trisamudrapitapoyavahana' (whose horses drank water from three seas), 'Ekabrahmana' (peerless Brahmin), 'Kshatriya-darpa-man-mardana' (destroyer of Kshatriya pride).
Consolidated eastern Andhra capital at Dhanyakataka (Dharanikota/Amaravati); Ptolemy refers to him as 'Siriptolemaios' ruling from Baithan (Paithan).
Coins featuring ship motifs with double masts
Champion of maritime commerce and naval expansion; patronized Mahayana Buddhist philosopher Acharya Nagarjuna at Sriparvata (Nagarjunakonda).

content.text: Socio-Economic Life: Society was patriarchal yet honored maternal lineage (matronymics like Gautamiputra, Vasishthiputra). Guilds (Srenis - e.g., Kolika/weavers, Tilapisaka/oil-pressers, Kamara/ironsmiths) functioned as commercial cartels and autonomous banks. Overseas trade with the Roman Empire flourished through eastern ports: Motupalli, Ghantasala (Kantakosila), Maisolia (Machilipatnam), and Koddura, bringing enormous influxes of Roman gold and silver denarii (unearthed at Vinukonda and Vidyadharapuram).

content.caption: Reconstructed model of the Great Stupa (Mahachaitya) of Amaravati, built during the Satavahana-Ikshvaku era with carved white palnad limestone panels depicting Jataka tales in dynamic narrative relief.
content.alt_text: Model of the Amaravati Stupa at Amaravati Archaeological Museum

content.caption: Successor Dynasties of Ancient Andhra: Political Centers and Contributions
rows: Kings performed Vedic sacrifices (Ashvamedha, Agnihotra), while royal ladies (Chantisri, Bhatideva) generously patronized Buddhism, building Mahachaityas and Viharas at Vijayapuri. Issued earliest Sanskrit inscriptions in South India (Ehuvala Santamula's reign). Reached by Roman merchants.

Hastivarman was defeated but liberated by Samudragupta during his southern expedition (recorded in Allahabad Pillar Inscription). Devotees of Chitrarathaswami (Sun God); their royal emblem was the Bull (Nandi).

Madhavavarma II ('Lord of Trikuta and Malaya') performed 11 Ashvamedhas, 1000 Agnishtomas, and Purushamedha (human sacrifice). Excavated rock-cut cave temples at Undavalli (four-storeyed cave featuring colossal reclining Anantasayana Vishnu) and Mogalrajapuram (Vijayawada). Royal emblem: Lion. Authored metric treatise 'Janasraya Chhandas'.
Issued Prakrit charters: Mayidavolu copper plate (mentioning 'Andhrapatha' with headquarters at Dhanyakataka) and British Museum (Hirahadagalli) copper plate.

content.text: 3. The Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (624–1075 CE) & Telugu Linguistic Awakening

Founded by Kubja Vishnuvardhana (brother of Badami Chalukya Pulakesin II) in 624 CE, the Eastern Chalukyas ruled Vengi for over four centuries, shaping the emergence of standard Telugu script, grammar, and literature:

items: Linguistic Evolution: Inscriptions progressively transitioned from Sanskrit and Prakrit to Telugu. Gunaga Vijayaditya's general Panduranga issued the Addanki Inscription (848 CE), featuring the earliest recorded Telugu verse meter (Taruvoja).

Rajaraja Narendra (1022–1061 CE) & Nannaya Bhattu: Rajaraja Narendra established his capital at Rajamahendravaram (Rajahmundry) along the Godavari. He commissioned his court poet Nannaya Bhattu (Adi Kavi) to translate Vyasa's Sanskrit Mahabharata into Telugu. Nannaya completed the Adi Parva, Sabha Parva, and part of Aranya Parva, inaugurating the classical Telugu literary tradition ('Andhra Mahabharatam') and earning the title 'Vaganusasana'.

Temple Architecture: Synthesis of Dravidian and Chalukyan idioms: Draksharama Bhimeswara Temple, Chalukya Kumararama Bhimeswara Temple at Samalkot, and the Golingeshwara Temple at Biccavolu (East Godavari).

Socio-Religious Transformation: Buddhism and Jainism declined sharply, replaced by Shaivism (specifically the worship of Pancharama Kshetras: Amararama/Amaravati, Draksharama, Kumararama/Samalkot, Bhimarama/Samalkot, Somarama/Gunupudi-Bhimavaram, Ksheerarama/Palakollu).

content.text: 4. Renati Cholas & The Earliest Telugu Stone Inscription

Ruling the Renadu region (modern YSR Kadapa and Chittoor districts) from the 5th to 8th century CE, the Renati Cholas claimed descent from Karikala Chola. In 575 CE, King Erikal Mutthuraju Dhanunjaya issued the famous Kalamalla Inscription (at Kalamalla village, YSR Kadapa district). This stands as the earliest epigraph written entirely in the Telugu language, proving that Telugu had crystallized into a distinct administrative and public medium by the 6th century CE.
5. Buddhism and Jainism in Ancient Andhra

content.caption: Prominent Buddhist and Jaina Centers in Ancient Andhra Pradesh
rows: Greatest Buddhist Mahachaitya in South India; birthplace of the Chaityavada / Purvasaila school of Mahasanghikas; epicenter of Amaravati School of Art characterized by marble/limestone narrative relief sculptures.

Residence of Acharya Nagarjuna (founder of Madhyamaka / Sunyavada Mahayana philosophy); complex of Mahachaitya, university, monastic amphitheater, and multi-sectarian viharas for monks from Ceylon, Gandhara, and China.
Site of ancient Stupa yielding caskets with relics; the Bhattiprolu script (a regional variant of southern Brahmi) represents the paleographic ancestor of the Telugu-Kannada script.
Unique monolithic and structural Buddhist site exhibiting Hinayana, Mahayana, and Vajrayana (Tantric) phases from 3rd century BCE to 9th century CE.
Rock-cut Buddhist monastery and circular chaitya griha often described as the 'Ajanta of Andhra'.

Patronized by Eastern Chalukya king Kubja Vishnuvardhana's wife Ayyana Mahadevi (built Nadumba Vasadi at Vijayawada); celebrated Acharya Kundakunda (founder of Mula Sangha, authored Samayasara) flourished in the Konakondla hills of Anantapur.

content.text: Part A: Mains Analytical & Descriptive Questions

items:
Trace the socio-economic conditions and maritime commercial supremacy of the Satavahana Empire in Andhra. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Introduce Satavahana chronology and core Andhra territories (Dhanyakataka); examine socioeconomic fabric (matronymic honor, merchant guilds/Srenis, caste fluidity); elaborate on maritime prosperity (ports of Maisolia, Motupalli, Ghantasala; ship-marked coins of Yajna Sri Satakarni; extensive Roman trade verified by periplus accounts and gold coin hoards); conclude on how agrarian stability and trade wealth funded the exquisite Amaravati school of art.

Assess the role of the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi in the development of the Telugu language, script, and literature. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Highlight transition from bilingualism to vernacular empowerment; analyze the Addanki inscription (848 CE) and its poetic Taruvoja meter; detail Rajaraja Narendra's royal court at Rajamahendravaram and his patronage of Nannaya Bhattu; examine Nannaya's Andhra Mahabharatam as the foundational bedrock of classical Telugu literature; discuss the architectural evolution of the Pancharama Shaivite temples.

Critically evaluate the significance of Nagarjunakonda and Amaravati as international seats of Buddhist philosophy and sculpture. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Introduce the Krishna river valley as the heart of Buddhism in peninsular India; analyze Amaravati's Mahachaitya and distinct sculptural style (naturalistic, white limestone, dynamic compositions depicting Jatakas); detail Nagarjunakonda's university complex, international viharas (Sinhala Vihara), and the philosophical revolution of Acharya Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka/Sunyavada system; conclude on its transmission across Southeast Asia.

content.text: Part B: Screening / Prelims Objective Questions

items:
Q1. Which Satavahana monarch issued the famous collection of Prakrit verses titled 'Gathasaptasati' (Gaha Sattasai)?
(a) Satakarni I
(b) Hala
(c) Gautamiputra Satakarni
(d) Yajna Sri Satakarni
Correct Answer: (b) Hala [Explanation: King Hala, the 17th Satavahana ruler, compiled Gathasaptasati in Maharashtri Prakrit, which contains several early Telugu indigenous words.]

Q2. The earliest recorded stone inscription written entirely in the Telugu language is the:
(a) Addanki Inscription of Panduranga
(b) Kalamalla Inscription of Erikal Mutthuraju Dhanunjaya
(c) Kurkyala Inscription of Jinavallabha
(d) Bezwada Inscription of Yuddhamalla
Correct Answer: (b) Kalamalla Inscription of Erikal Mutthuraju Dhanunjaya [Explanation: Discovered in Kalamalla village, YSR Kadapa district, this Renati Chola inscription dates to 575 CE and is the earliest stone epigraph written entirely in Telugu.]

Q3. The famous Undavalli cave temples near Vijayawada featuring the colossal four-storeyed reclining Anantasayana Vishnu were excavated by which dynasty?
(a) Satavahanas
(b) Ikshvakus
(c) Vishnukundins
(d) Eastern Chalukyas
Correct Answer: (c) Vishnukundins [Explanation: The Vishnukundin dynasty excavated the rock-cut cave temples of Undavalli and Mogalrajapuram in the 5th-6th century CE.]

Q4. Which Eastern Chalukyan ruler patronized Nannaya Bhattu to translate the Sanskrit Mahabharata into Telugu?
(a) Kubja Vishnuvardhana
(b) Gunaga Vijayaditya
(c) Rajaraja Narendra
(d) Danarnava
Correct Answer: (c) Rajaraja Narendra [Explanation: Rajaraja Narendra (1022–1061 CE) ruled from Rajamahendravaram and requested Nannaya Bhattu to compose the Andhra Mahabharatam.]

Q5. Acharya Nagarjuna, the propounder of the Madhyamaka (Sunyavada) school of Mahayana Buddhism, was a contemporary and friend of which Satavahana monarch?
(a) Simuka
(b) Gautamiputra Satakarni
(c) Yajna Sri Satakarni
(d) Hala
Correct Answer: (c) Yajna Sri Satakarni [Explanation: Tibetan and Chinese records, alongside Bana's Harshacharita, record that Acharya Nagarjuna resided at Sriparvata (Nagarjunakonda) under the patronage of Yajna Sri Satakarni.]
